lesson_title: Count the World, Count Your Wish: The Counting Principle
hook_text: What are the chances a random 5-digit code has no repeated digit? Most people guess half. The real answer is sneakier.
clip_script: Your phone wants a 5-digit unlock code. How many are possible? Do not list them — draw five dashes, one per digit, ten options above each, and multiply: one hundred thousand. Now the sharper question: how many use five DIFFERENT digits? Same dashes, but the numbers shrink as digits get spent: 10, then 9, then 8, then 7, then 6. Multiply: thirty thousand two hundred and forty. So the probability a random code repeats nothing is 30 240 over 100 000 — 0,3024. Under a third. Repeats sneak in far more often than five short digits suggest. That is the whole topic in one move: count the world for the bottom, count your wish for the top, divide. Photos run on the same engine: five debaters line up, 5 factorial, 120 line-ups. Two cousins glued together? Four units times the swap inside the knot — 48. Chance they land side by side at random: two fifths. Dashes, shrinking numbers, one clean fraction. No listing, ever.
visual_style: A glowing phone lock screen, five dashes filling with spinning digits, option counters ticking down from 10 to 6, then a debate-team photo row with two cousins snapping together on an elastic string.
mood: Quick-fingered, game-show energy, one genuinely surprising statistic.
pacing: Rapid dash-filling beats, a pause on the 0,3024 reveal, playful bounce through the photo row finish.
call_to_action: Watch the full lesson and count anything without listing a single case.
